A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same IT3 research work. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original IT3 experiments on tabular regression, corrupted-image classification, age prediction, road segmentation, and aerodynamic prediction, including online adaptation and appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains original experimental results and adds ImageNet-C evaluation, comparator results, idempotence diagnostics, and inference-time and memory measurements.

M1.justification: The auxiliary label input, supervised training loss, frozen-reference test-time loss, batch resetting, and online EMA variant remain unchanged. The expanded method discussion and appendices explain these procedures without establishing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v2 adds large-scale ImageNet/ImageNet-C classification coverage in Section 4.7. Conversely, v1 Appendix A.1's separate evaluation on RoadTracer cities excluded from training disappears. The other datasets and principal task scenarios remain represented.

E2.justification: v1 principally compares against non-adapted models, with TTT included for CIFAR-C. v2 adds ActMAD comparisons for tabular data, CIFAR-C, roads, airfoils, and cars, and adds TTT to road segmentation. Its new ImageNet-C comparison evaluates TENT, ETA, MEMO, and ActMAD. Despite broader wording in Section 4, the age-prediction figure still shows only the non-adapted model and IT3.

E3.justification: The reported CIFAR-C TTT settings change from one instance augmented to 32 examples in v1 to batches of 8, 32, and 128 in v2. New ImageNet-C experiments use ResNet-18, 15 corruption types, five severity levels, and batches of 16–128. Appendix A adds relative inference-time comparisons and peak reserved GPU-memory measurement at batch 128.

E4.justification: v2 adds airfoil idempotence-error distributions before and after adaptation, an ImageNet-C accuracy-versus-idempotence analysis, and computational-cost comparisons. Its appendix segmentation montage compares TTT, ActMAD, and IT3 with per-example quality scores, replacing v1's additional iteration-progress examples. These substantially expand diagnostic and supplementary evidence without introducing component ablations.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 15 introduces Pearson correlation estimation across inference batches to quantify the relationship between idempotence error and accuracy. Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the statistical addition does not establish improved run-to-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds ImageNet-C and comparator outcomes, a Pearson correlation of -0.94, and resource results: IT3 inference costs 4×, 5×, and 6× the base model for airfoils, cars, and roads, respectively, and uses 7.4 GB in the ImageNet-C memory comparison. Table 1 is unchanged, including online road quality 69.8, airfoil MAE 34.1, and car MAE 0.385. The held-out-city RoadTracer results are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit joint fixed-point-set formulation and categorical claims that the residual is zero in-distribution and positive for OOD inputs, extending v1's approximate consistency relation and possible OOD deviations. Most Appendix C equations restate existing mathematics. No general theorem or proof connecting self-consistency to prediction correctness is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains domain-independent test-time adaptation through idempotence. However, v2's abstract newly claims a theoretical connection to prediction confidence and consistent superiority over existing approaches, extending v1's emphasis on versatility across tasks and architectures.

C2.justification: The new appendices substantially develop the internal-representation projection interpretation and assert that small residuals indicate reliable predictions. Meanwhile, v2 removes v1's explicit CIFAR single-instance failure discussion, the explanation that the objective lacks independent input information, and the qualification that domain-specific methods may outperform IT3. A shorter general single-instance limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies code and project links absent from v1 and newly discloses typical adaptation of 1–3 optimization steps and the CUDA peak-memory measurement function. These additions improve documentation but do not establish changed update budgets for retained experiments. Most existing architecture and training details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through ActMAD, depth-completion adaptation, a TTA survey, and ETA/MEMO references. Section 2.1 adds an explicit TTT-versus-TTA distinction and recognizes ActMAD's potential across modalities, replacing v1's position that suitable adaptation comparators were unavailable outside classification. The relationship to IGN receives extensive additional discussion.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, the introduction and method exposition are extensively revised, and the experimental comparison narrative changes throughout. Separate limitations and conclusion sections become a combined section with a different future-work emphasis. New explanatory appendices and an impact statement substantially reshape the document's narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main-text layout and extensively redesigns comparative plots, legends, and colors. Separate mean-error plots are removed while corresponding boxplots remain; new diagnostic and ImageNet-C figures and four resource tables are added. The appendix's road displays are replaced by a cross-method segmentation montage.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's central empirical weakness: reliance mainly on non-adapted baselines and an explicitly mismatched CIFAR TTT comparison. Broader evaluated competitors, aligned reported CIFAR batch sizes, ImageNet-C validation, and resource measurements make the method's benefits and costs much easier to assess. These gains outweigh the removed held-out-city experiment and shortened limitations, although the stronger appendix claims about reliability exceed what self-consistency alone establishes.
